Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for New Zealand's reply with the bat. Devon Conway and Tim Robinson walk out to open for the Blackcaps. The players of West Indies spread out to take their fielding positions. Jayden Seales has the new ball and is raring to go. Robinson to face. Off we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Well then, 165 is the magic number for New Zealand to chase and take an early lead in the series. For that, they need a stable start against the new ball. Devon Conway hasn't been in good form lately and if West Indies manage to exploit the conditions well and get a couple of wickets inside the Powerplay, they could really dent through their batting order. But it all depends on who wins the execution battle here at Eden Park, as batting under the lights gets a bit easy. Won't be an easy job for the visitors against a power-packed batting lineup of New Zealand. Back in a bit for the chase.

New Zealand's Jacob Duffy is in for a chat with the broadcasters. He says he’s happy with his effort and 164 is a total they would have taken at the start of the game. Believes that the wicket is a bit two-paced and some balls were holding in the surface. Reckons that they bowled well as a unit and made it hard for West Indies to score.

New Zealand were spot on to exploit the conditions. With the new ball, they threw a trial by pace, and once the ball got older, cutters and spin variations were unleashed to near-perfection in that middle phase, which made timing the ball really tricky. However, they were a bit sloppy in the field as several chances were shelled. Chase and Powell worked hard towards the backend, with the latter being the heavy lifter in that 49-run partnership. But they lost both of them in no time as West Indies slipped from 146/4 to 148/6. But thanks to their contributions and the lower order stepping up, they still managed to score 51 runs off the last five overs.

The schedule in international cricket shows no mercy. Just a few moons back, West Indies were battling on low, slow tracks in Bangladesh, where the ball barely got above shin height. Now they've landed in New Zealand, where the same delivery rears up chest-high. It's a brutal adjustment to make in such a short turnaround. It was Shai Hope, the only batter who looked assured with that adjustment, and he went on to score a classy fifty and formed a much-needed partnership with Chase before perishing.

When in New Zealand, the ball skids, jagging sideways with a sharp bounce to keep the batters honest. Brandon King struggled to get going, while Alick Athanaze looked fluent with a couple of crisp boundaries before throwing it away. The early movement and extra bounce proved too much for the West Indies openers to handle. New Zealand's pace attack was clinical in their execution, keeping things tight and picking up crucial wickets to peg the visitors back to 32/2 at the end of the Powerplay.

West Indies will be quite happy with the kind of finish they got. Honestly, they were way behind the eight ball in the Powerplay, but have made a good comeback to post a total which is in touching distance of the average first inning score at Eden Park. New Zealand bowled well for 80 percent of the innings, but won't be pleased with the death bowling. They dropped a few chances, missed a couple of run out chances that really might have dented the scoring even further.

Commentary.Commentary: The crowd is gradually building up, and let's hope we are treated to a cracker of a game. Mitchell Santner leads his troops out to the centre. They are followed by the two Windies' openers, Brandon King and Alick Athanaze. Jacob Duffy will kickstart proceedings with the new ball. Duffy to King with a slip in place. Here we go!

We are moments away from the first ball, but before that, the two teams will line up for the national anthems. It will be the West Indies' anthem first, followed by the national anthem of New Zealand.

The captain of West Indies, Shai Hope, says they would have bowled first as well and reckons that it will get better to bat as the evening progresses. Stresses that they will have to put big runs on the board. Informs that they have got a couple of spinners and a few seamers. Overall, he says it is a pretty mixed bag.

New Zealand's captain, Mitchell Santner, admits that while winning the series remains their main objective, the team also has one eye on the World Cup and fine-tuning their preparations. He cheekily adds that the conditions in Auckland will be quite different from what they can expect in India.
West Indies (Playing XI) - Brandon King, Alick Athanaze, Shai Hope (C/WK), Roston Chase, Ackeem Auguste, Rovman Powell, Jason Holder, Romario Shepherd, Matthew Forde, Akeal Hosein, and Jayden Seales.

New Zealand (Playing XI) - Tim Robinson, Devon Conway (WK), Rachin Ravindra, Mark Chapman, Daryl Mitchell, Michael Bracewell, James Neesham, Mitchell Santner (C), Zakary Foulkes, Kyle Jamieson, and Jacob Duffy.
TOSS - The flip of the coin lands in favor of New Zealand, and Mitchell Santner has elected to BOWL first.

This is the first meeting between these two sides in this format since the T20 World Cup 2024, where the Men in Maroon defeated the Blackcaps. Overall though, New Zealand hold a clear edge with a 10-5 head-to-head record, and at home, they have been pretty dominant with a 7-1 lead. Interestingly, it's at this very venue, Eden Park, where two of the four matches between these teams have ended in ties. So expect the unexpected here. Luckily, there is no rain forecast and the weather is clear and windy in Auckland, so we are all in for a complete game of cricket. Toss and team sheets coming up shortly.

Over in the West Indies camp, injuries have depleted the pace attack. Frontline seamers Shamar Joseph and Alzarri Joseph are both still sidelined due to injuries, and the burden to lead this department falls on Jayden Seales, who hasn’t disappointed much so far. Matthew Forde returns to support him, and so does Shamar Springer. Stability at the top order has been a long-standing concern for the Windies, but their recent tour of the subcontinent might have sorted that out. Skipper Shai Hope, young Alick Athanaze, and dynamic Brandon King all delivered solid returns, giving them what looks like the right pecking order. That's a huge relief heading into a World Cup year. There was a desperate need for controlled aggression up top, with merciless power hitters ready to explode in the middle order. That blueprint seems to be falling into place now, but it is all about sustainability.

The injury bug won't leave New Zealand alone. Tim Seifert fractured his finger playing for Northern Districts in the Ford Trophy, so he's out of action. Canterbury’s Mitchell Hay gets his chance as the replacement keeper. Losing in-form Seifert means more weight on the shoulders of Devon Conway, Tim Robinson, and Rachin Ravindra to fortify the top order for competitive totals. At least the bowling looks solid. And in the absence of Matt Henry, the load to lead this pace unit is on Jacob Duffy, along with Zakary Foulkes. The rest of the squad is basically what we saw against England, with Ish Sodhi added back in for some leg spin. He will operate alongside skipper Mitchell Santner's left-arm orthodox, and Auckland is also known for offering a bit of assistance to the spinners too.

Three months or so until the next T20 World Cup. That's all the time left, and suddenly every game feels like it counts double. West Indies are coming in hot. They just swept Bangladesh in the T20Is and look like a team that's figured things out. Confidence is high, and they'll fancy their chances in this part of the world as well. New Zealand? Not so much. They've lost back-to-back T20I series at home - first to Australia, then England, although with the weather’s interference in both assignments, with just three completed games out of six, but with zero wins. It's been a bit rough, and now they will aim to fix the loose ends with a quick turnaround.

Hello, cricket addicts! Fresh day, fresh series, and we're locked in. Cricket never sleeps, never slows. Bet no one's complaining, eh? England's white-ball tour has just wrapped, and now, fresh off their successful Bangladesh assignment, the men from the Caribbean march into Kiwi land for an all-format tour starting with a highly anticipated 5-match T20I series. It all kicks off here in the 'City of Sails', Auckland, at the iconic Eden Park. On that note, we welcome you all to our coverage of the first T20I between New Zealand and West Indies. Let's get right into it.
... MATCH DAY ...

A thrilling five-match T20I series is on the horizon as Mitchell Santner-led New Zealand hosts the West Indies in Auckland, with the home side looking to bounce back from recent setbacks against England and Australia, in the T20I format, while Shai Hope's men are riding high on the momentum of a whitewash victory over Bangladesh. New Zealand will be without the services of Kane Williamson, who has hung up his boots for the shorter format, but they'll welcome back the experienced Ish Sodhi, who missed the England series. Meanwhile, West Indies will be buoyed by the return of Matthew Forde, who has overcome a shoulder injury, and the inclusion of Shamar Springer, who adds depth to their pace attack in the absence of Ramon Simmons and Jediah Blades. With both teams evenly matched, the West Indies' current form in T20Is could prove decisive, but New Zealand will be keen to capitalize on their home advantage and exploit the vulnerabilities of their opponents, setting the stage for an enthralling contest between two cricketing heavyweights.
